They are 30% to 70% more efficient than traditional separate on- site heat generation and grid power [32]. In large-scale district energy applications, the new CHPmodelmustsatisfytwokeyrequirements. First,themodelshouldbephysics-basedand capableofcapturingthedynamicbehaviorofthermodynamicvariables,includingmassflow and enthalpy variations in liquid water and saturated steam, while also calculating power generation. Second,itmustremaincomputationallyefficientbyavoidingdiscontinuitiesand reducingthepresenceofnonlinearequationsystems,ensuringstableandfastsimulations. To meet the requirements, two main approaches are employed to increase the simulation speed while maintaining acceptable accuracy in district energy applications. The first ap- 53 proach is the split-medium [33] method. Separates the water and steam mediums into two different medium models, avoiding numerical discontinuities and nonlinearities when simu- lating phase changes from water to steam. The model using this approach is available in the Modelica Buildings Library [31]. The second approach uses empirical correlation functions or look-up tables to compute essential physical variables and thermal efficiencies, captur- ing thermodynamic properties and energy conversion processes. This eliminates the need to calculate the nonlinear thermodynamic properties of superheated steam, thereby enhancing the simulation speed. The application of these two approaches leads to differences between the simplified CHP model and the actual physical system.
